newsitem.title: GERMANY: Anti-soya protest continues after Hamburg port action.
newsitem.headline: Anti-soya protest continues after Hamburg port action.

text.p: Greenpeace environmentalists picketed a freighter which arrived on Tuesday with what is believed to be the first cargo genetically-altered U.S. soybeans to arrive in Europe and said their protests would continue.

A Greenpeace barge and two inflatable dingies accompanied the Ideal Progress, with 44,600 tonnes of new crop soybeans for German processor Oelmuehle Hamburg (Oelag), on the stormy River Elbe for some three hours.

"Oelag gave consumers no choice...it will go ahead and process the beans for the feed industry and for human consumption and unfortunately for export," said activist Michael Kuehn on board the Greenpeace barge Beluga.
"We will monitor where Oelag sends its products and we will ask its customers to stop accepting them."
Police and port authorities would not allow Greenpeace to prevent the cargo from being unloaded and, as four tugboats pulled the freighter into position, told the Beluga to leave.

The environmentalists emblazoned slogans, reading "Genetic soya is only the beginning," "Genetic Experiment -- don't buy it," and "We're not your guinea pigs," onto the side of the ship from slide projectors during the trip.

About one to two percent of the U.S. soybean crop is now made up of genetically-altered beans and Greenpeace said it was likely that some of this was aboard the Ideal Progress, which left New Orleans 20 days ago.
Its cargo will take two days to be sucked into silos. The processed soy oil and meal will leave Oelag from November 10.
Health anxieties about biotechnology are most acute in Germany, where Greenpeace has gathered 120,000 signatories on a consumer petition against modified soybeans.
Developed by U.S. chemicals giant Monsanto Co, the soybeans have been altered to resist widely-used Roundup weedkiller.
Campaigners want crushers to segregate these beans and the food industry either to boycott them or at least to label products that might be derived from them.
Soya is used in some form or another in about 30,000 foodstuffs including margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
U.S. consumer activist Jeremy Rifkin, who seeks a world boycott of genetically-altered grain, arrived in Germany on Tuesday to declare that "this global boycott will not go away."

He said brokers in the U.S. Midwest were already negotiating contracts for a gene-free supply with European processors who did not want Monsanto soy and an initial cargo would sail from Duluth, Minn. in the United States on Tuesday or Wednesday.
The Ideal Progress and the ship leaving Duluth symbolised rival approaches to the future of farm and food policy, he said.
Some leading firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have said they will not sell products with oils from modified beans, but they consider the beans safe.
But the Food and Drink Industry Association in the Netherlands, where cargoes will also be landed this month, said in a statement that members would use genetically-altered soya.
It said health authorities in the United States, Britain, the European Union, Canada and Japan had also approved the product.
The United States sold two million tonnes of soybeans worth $690 million to Germany last year and Argentina plans to use modified beans in 1997.
Traders said it was possible to buy soy oil guaranteed not to have been made with such beans but cost was a problem.
The Iowa-based firm of Genetic ID, for instance, says it can detect whether foreign DNA has been spliced into soybeans.
But traders said the tests plus separate transport and storage added about $15 per tonne to the cost of soybeans shipped to Europe. Current prices are around $276 per tonne.
